When I make a verbal offer to a senior candidate, I expect a conversation, not just a yes. What I do not expect is a list. The candidates who handle it well pick two points, no more, and they attach a condition to each one. They tell me they could accept the base, provided that something else moves. They tell me what is non-negotiable for them, and they let me find the middle ground. The ones who handle it badly say yes on the phone and then send me ten changes by email. Unless there is a very good reason, I would rather hear every condition on the call, so I can take it to the board in one go.

When I was offered my current job, I nearly made a mistake. I was so pleased that I almost accepted on the call. Instead, I asked for a day and wrote down what really mattered: the reporting line and the shares. The salary was fine. The next morning I said I would sign, as long as the shares vested over three years instead of five. The chief executive said that was too much, and we met halfway at four. To sweeten the deal, she added a small sign-on bonus that I had not even asked for. My advice is simple: know the one thing you would walk away for, and be flexible about everything else.

Finally, he agrees to start in March, on condition that everything is in writing by Friday.
